Insolvent

in-SOL-vunt -- stress on the second syllable, SOL. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Insolvent is unable to pay the debts one owes.

By December the toy company was insolvent, owing far more to its suppliers than its shops could ever bring in.

Worked Example

A family restaurant has forty thousand dollars in unpaid bills, eight hundred dollars in the bank, and no way to pay this month's food delivery.

The restaurant is insolvent: what it owes is simply beyond what it can pay. Now look at how the word is built -- solvent, which you already learned earlier in this course, means 'able to pay one's debts.' Put this unit's prefix in front of it and in-solvent flips straight into the opposite. This is the cleanest example of the whole unit: a real taught word, a real prefix, an exact reversal.

How Insolvent Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

bankrupt

bankrupt: officially declared unable to pay what one owes

broke

broke: informal: having no money left

ruined

ruined: financially destroyed

Antonyms

solvent

solvent: able to pay one's debts -- the exact word this unit's prefix reverses, and one you already learned earlier in this course

prosperous

prosperous: financially successful and thriving

How Strong Is It? — broke → insolvent → bankrupt

broke vs. insolvent

broke vs. insolvent: Broke is the casual, temporary version -- a student is broke until payday -- while an insolvent business owes more than it can ever pay back.

bankrupt vs. insolvent

bankrupt vs. insolvent: Bankrupt is insolvency made official: insolvency is the condition of being unable to pay, while bankruptcy is the legal declaration a court makes about it.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin in-)

root — solvent

root — solvent: able to pay one's debts (Latin solvere 'to loosen, to release, to pay off')

Put it together

Put it together: Insolvent is this unit's flagship word, because both halves are real, taught English: in- ('not') plus solvent ('able to pay your debts'), a word from earlier in this course. Latin solvere meant 'to loosen' -- paying a debt loosens the tie between you and the person you owe. Someone insolvent cannot loosen that tie at all.

Word Choice

Keep this pair together in your memory: solvent = able to pay, insolvent = unable to pay. They are the same word with this unit's prefix flipping the meaning, and the ISEE loves exactly that kind of pair. Insolvent belongs to businesses, estates, and banks more often than to people, and its noun is insolvency.
